title: Hurricanes and Typhoons
objective: After this level you can explain how tropical storms form and why they have different names in different oceans.
summary: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are one kind of storm, named by ocean. They feed on warm water, spin with the Coriolis effect and weaken over land.

cards.headline: A hurricane, a typhoon and a cyclone walk into a bar. They are the same storm.
cards.body: They're all tropical cyclones. The only difference between them is where on the ocean the storm happens.

cards.headline: Built on warm water
cards.body: A tropical cyclone starts over ocean water of about 27°C (80°F) or warmer. The water evaporates, and warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses into towering clouds. Once its sustained winds reach 119 km/h (74 mph), it's officially a hurricane or typhoon. Push it over land and it's cut off from its warm, moist ocean air, so its winds weaken. No warm water, no fuel.

cards.headline: The spin comes from Earth
cards.body: Here's Level 33's Coriolis effect again. It makes these storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. But the Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator, so a storm there has nothing to get it spinning. That's why tropical cyclones form some distance away from the Equator, even though the water there is plenty warm.

cards.headline: Storm names: decoded
learned: Hurricane, typhoon, cyclone: one storm, named by ocean
They need ocean water of about 27°C or warmer
Over land they lose their fuel and weaken
Coriolis spins them; it is zero at the Equator

questions.prompt: Match each region with the name its tropical cyclones get.
questions.explanation: In the North Atlantic it's a hurricane, in the Northwest Pacific a typhoon, and in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific a cyclone.

questions.prompt: Why does a hurricane weaken after it moves over land?

options.label: It's cut off from its warm, moist ocean air
The Coriolis effect stops working over land
options.rationale: The Coriolis effect works everywhere except right at the Equator.

options.label: Land air is too humid for it
options.rationale: Humid ocean air is its fuel.

options.label: Mountains always split it in two
options.rationale: The key loss is its warm ocean fuel.

questions.explanation: Hurricanes run on warm, moist air rising off warm ocean water. Over land that supply is cut off.

questions.prompt: Using Level 33: tropical cyclones don't form right on the Equator because _____.

options.label: the water there is too cold
options.rationale: The Equator's water is warm enough.

options.label: trade winds blow them apart
options.rationale: Trade winds are not what stops them.

options.label: air pressure is always high
options.rationale: Heating makes pressure low near the Equator.

questions.explanation: A storm needs the Coriolis effect to start spinning, and at the Equator it's zero.
